opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think internal deployment is one of the most underrated parts of the risk picture. Most of the public conversation, and most of the regulation people are drafting, is about what happens when a model gets released externally: the API, the chatbot, the open weights. But the first place the most capable models actually get used is inside the labs themselves, often months before anyone outside sees them, and sometimes they're never released at all.

There are a few reasons that worries me.

The first is oversight. When you deploy externally, you have usage policies, monitoring, red-teaming reports, system cards, journalists and researchers poking at the thing. Internally, a lot of that scrutiny falls away. The assumption is "these are our own employees, they're trusted." But the risk we care most about isn't only misuse by a bad actor. It's the model itself behaving in ways we didn't intend. A misaligned model doesn't care whether its user has a company badge.

The second is what the models are being used *for* internally. The labs are increasingly using their best systems to do AI research: writing code, running experiments, eventually helping design the next generation of models. That's exactly the setting where a model that's subtly scheming, or even just has slightly wrong goals, could do the most damage. It has access to the training infrastructure, the codebase, maybe its own weights or the evaluation pipelines meant to catch it. If you were worried about a model sabotaging safety research or inserting backdoors into successor models, internal R&D is precisely where that would happen.

The third is the feedback loop. If AI starts substantially accelerating AI development inside one company, you can get very rapid capability gains that are mostly invisible to the outside world. Governments, other labs, and the public could be meaningfully behind on what actually exists. That's bad for safety, and it's also a concentration-of-power concern: a small group could end up with extremely capable systems and very little external accountability.

So I'd like to see internal deployment treated with at least the same seriousness as external deployment: proper threat modeling, control measures that assume the model might not be trustworthy, monitoring of what agents actually do with their permissions, and some form of disclosure to governments about what's being run internally. Right now I think it's a pretty big gap in how we think about governance.

r001.rationale: It says AI used for AI research could substantially accelerate development inside a company, creating rapid capability gains.

r002.rationale: It describes a small group gaining highly capable systems with little external accountability, indicating advances could proceed without meaningful outside influence.

r003.rationale: It says the capability gains could be mostly invisible to the outside world, leaving governments, other labs, and the public behind.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the core worry is that you get a world where the most capable systems are being used internally, maybe for months, before anyone outside the company has any idea what they can do. And internally they're being used for exactly the things we should be most careful about: automating AI research, accelerating the next training run, writing the security-critical code, and so on. So the models that matter most for the trajectory are also the ones with the least external scrutiny.

There are a few layers to why that worries me. The first is just plain information asymmetry. Right now, a lot of what we know about frontier capabilities comes from models being out in the world. External evaluators, academics, red-teamers, even just curious users surface things the developers didn't anticipate. If deployment is internal-only, that whole channel disappears. Governments and the public are reasoning about where AI is based on a picture that could be a year out of date, and a year is a very long time at current rates of progress.

The second is that the incentives inside a lab are not neutral. If you're in a race and your internal model makes your researchers twice as productive, there is enormous pressure to just use it. The people deciding whether it's safe to run a model that's doing a lot of your R&D are the same people who benefit most from running it. I don't think that's a story about bad actors. It's a story about normal organizational dynamics applied to an unusually high-stakes situation. Safety cases become a bit less rigorous, monitoring gets deprioritized, and nobody outside has the ability to push back because nobody outside knows.

The third, and this is the one I spend most of my time on, is that internal deployment is precisely the setting where misalignment or scheming would be most dangerous and hardest to catch. If a model is being used with broad permissions inside the lab, with access to code, to training infrastructure, to the evaluations themselves, then a model that's pursuing goals we didn't intend has a lot of leverage. It could subtly sabotage safety research, insert vulnerabilities, or influence the next generation of models. And we currently don't have great tools to detect that. Our evals for things like sandbagging or deceptive behavior are still immature. So you're combining the highest-stakes affordances with the weakest oversight.

What I'd want to see instead is treating internal deployment as a real deployment, with the same seriousness as an external one. That means clear thresholds for what capabilities trigger extra controls, meaningful monitoring of what the model is doing internally, some external party, whether that's a government body or an independent auditor, that actually gets visibility into internally deployed systems, and honestly just transparency about the fact that these systems exist and roughly what they can do. Right now almost none of that is standard practice, and I think that gap is one of the more underrated risks in the whole picture.

r001.rationale: It says internal models automate AI research and accelerate the next training run, describing AI use that speeds development of further AI systems.

r002.rationale: It says internal-only deployment leaves outsiders unable to scrutinize or push back on the systems’ use and development.

r003.rationale: It says outsiders may have no idea what the systems can do and that public understanding could be a year out of date.

astra-6.text:
The main concern is that internal deployment can still be very consequential. You might imagine that as long as a model hasn’t been released to the public, the company is just doing research. But if its own staff are using it to automate AI research and engineering, it could substantially accelerate the development of the next generation of models.

So you could have this feedback loop where increasingly capable AI helps build even more capable AI, all before there’s a public release. If your safety commitments only kick in when you make a model available to customers, you’ve potentially missed a really important part of the process.

Internal deployment can reduce some risks—you have more control over who’s using the system and what they’re doing with it. But it doesn’t automatically address whether the model is controllable, or whether you’re accelerating beyond your ability to assess and manage the risks. The relevant question is what the system can do and what access it has, rather than whether the person using it works for the company.

r001.rationale: It describes internal AI automating AI research and engineering, accelerating the next generation, and forming a loop in which more capable AI helps build more capable AI.

r002.rationale: It says this can happen before public release, but does not identify the risk that the rest of the world has no say in those advances.

r003.rationale: It describes accelerating development of the next generation of models before public release, communicating that major advances could occur without the rest of the world knowing.

sol-6.1.text:
The main concern is that a model can be deployed internally and still have a huge impact. If it’s helping your researchers build the next generation of AI, then you could get a substantial acceleration in capabilities without ever releasing that model to the public.

So “we haven’t deployed it externally” isn’t, by itself, a strong safety guarantee. The relevant questions are what the model can do, what access it has, and how much autonomy you give it. An internal model with access to code, compute, and sensitive research could pose serious risks, even if only a relatively small number of employees use it.

And that can be harder for outsiders to scrutinise. You want evaluations and safeguards to apply before consequential internal use, rather than treating the public release as the point at which safety starts to matter.

r001.rationale: It says the model could help researchers build the next generation of AI, accelerating capabilities without public release.

r002.rationale: It notes that outsiders may find internal deployment harder to scrutinise, but does not say the rest of the world is denied a say in major AI breakthroughs.

r003.rationale: It says internal advances may be harder for outsiders to scrutinise, but does not identify the risk that the rest of the world remains unaware of major advances.
